Area.evidence_source: [/page/15/Text/6] This study suggests that participants' experiences of difficult emotions and their responses to intense negative emotions involved a complex and dynamic process of interactions that shaped negative self-perceptions and maladaptive coping strategies. Disturbing emotions were reported to dominate the lives of these individuals during the time they were suicidal, and participants' perceptions of becoming suicidal centered around three main themes of emotional experience: overwhelming despair, shame and selfloathing, and alienation. [/page/16/Text/3] It is interesting that shame was spontaneously discussed by our participants and was identified as contributing to the reinforcement of negative self-perceptions, self-loathing, lack of personal value, and anxiety. The experience of shame compelled participants to keep their negative emotions secret and served to restrain them from help-seeking behavior. [/page/16/Text/4] Consistent with this research, participants in this study reported suicidal ideation to act as a barrier to help-seeking behavior. It is important to note that participants attributed difficulties with help seeking to experiences of shame, worthlessness, and anxiety. Shame reactions acted to restrain suicidal individuals from both seeking help and expressing their needs, making them hypersensitive to negative attitudes of others and motivating an urge to flee and avoid being with other people (Wiklander et al., 2003). Consistent with Arnett (2004), who discusses the effect of leaving a distressing family situation, for the participants in this study, removal from the distressing environment, whether it was home, school, or community, often reduced the sense of vulnerability and allowed participants to recognize and use external resources that facilitated their healing. Little prior experience with intense negative emotions contributed to difficulties in expressing and dealing with emotions. However, once a trusting relationship was developed, openly discussing negative emotions provided participants with an expanded understanding of their experiences. [/page/17/Text/3] Many of those interviewed in this study described having families in which emotions were not expressed and personal feelings were ignored or kept hidden. They perceived their parents as failing to model emotional control and expression and neglecting to teach the value of emotional communication. These participants had difficulty describing their emotions while they were suicidal and lacked the vocabulary to describe emotional states. Their struggle to discriminate and differentiate between emotions contributed to feelings of helplessness that were not necessarily resolved within the family but were ameliorated when another significant relationship was established (Bostik & Everall, in press). [/page/17/Text/4] Affect dysregulation has been associated with suicidal behavior during adolescence, suggesting that youth who attempt suicide may have a diminished capacity to manage their internal states and may use suicide attempts as a means of reducing intolerable emotional states (Zlotnick et al., 1997). Reports of the experiences of participants in this study support this contention, as most perceived their intense, distressing emotions to dominate every aspect of their lives and saw no available relief other than suicide. When experiencing overwhelmingly negative emotions, participants tended to interpret difficulties with emotional regulation [/page/18/Text/2] and expression as signifying personal inadequacy. Increasingly, participants in this study focused on suicide as the only option that would save them from their intense negative emotional reality.
